Russia Imposes Temporary Export Ban on Select Chemical Products, Disrupting Industry

Russia’s Ministry of Industry and Trade has announced a temporary export ban on a range of key chemical products in response to tightening domestic supply and volatility in global prices, a move that is already sending ripples through the country’s chemicals industry.

The measure, which came into effect late last week and is set to last for an initial period of six months, covers a selection of basic and specialty chemicals including certain grades of polyethylene, polypropylene, and methanol derivatives. The government said the restriction is aimed at safeguarding domestic manufacturing, stabilizing local prices, and ensuring that Russian industries have sufficient access to essential raw materials.

Sibur Holding PAO, Russia’s largest petrochemical producer, is among the companies affected by the new policy. The company and its peers, such as the regional player Volzhsky ChemTech, have seen immediate impacts on export operations as shipments scheduled for overseas clients have been halted or rerouted.

“The export ban has created significant uncertainty for our planning and customer commitments abroad,” said a spokesperson for Sibur Holding PAO. “While we understand the government’s rationale, the abrupt implementation has led to logistical challenges and will likely affect our revenue projections for the second and third quarters.”

According to data released by the Russian Association of Chemical Manufacturers, exports of the affected chemicals accounted for approximately 18% of industry revenue last year. Market analysts estimate that companies could collectively lose up to $600 million in export sales if the ban remains in place for the full six months.

Local industry leaders are calling for more clarity and support from authorities. “We urge the government to engage in dialogue with manufacturers to mitigate the economic impact and consider a phased approach to any future restrictions,” said Viktor Lebedev, chair of the Russian Chemicals Trade Union.

The ban has also led to rapid changes in domestic pricing, with spot market prices for polyethylene and polypropylene falling by 8% since the announcement. Smaller producers, heavily reliant on exports, are reportedly facing cash flow difficulties and are seeking emergency credit lines to weather the disruption.

While the Ministry of Industry and Trade has signaled that it will review the measure in three months, officials insist the priority remains securing supply for Russian manufacturers. “This is a necessary step to protect our national interests in times of global uncertainty,” Deputy Minister Elena Rogozina said in a statement.

As the situation develops, industry participants remain on alert for further updates, closely monitoring both domestic market dynamics and the outcome of ongoing discussions with regulators.
